claims.text: Trace interstitial impurities combined with mechanical loading promote nanoscale phase segregation and precipitation in an initially single-phase HEA.
Impurity-associated segregation or precipitation occurs especially along grain boundaries.
The resulting segregated phases or precipitates reduce dislocation mobility.
The resulting segregated phases or precipitates reduce crack-tip blunting.
Impurity-induced segregation causes loss of toughness and a transition toward brittle fracture.
Testing near 700°C can activate impurity-driven phase segregation.
Service-relevant mechanical strain rates help activate impurity-driven phase segregation.
Trace oxygen or similar interstitials induce nanoscale precipitates or segregated phases.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen can initially contribute to solid-solution strengthening.
Elevated-temperature exposure can cause trace interstitials to promote phase segregation.
Mechanical deformation promotes impurity-driven phase segregation.
Phase segregation depletes solute interstitials from the metal matrix and causes matrix softening.
Segregation reduces plastic deformation by hindering dislocation movement.
Segregation limits crack-tip shielding and thereby facilitates brittle fracture.
Oxygen-doped specimens will have lower fracture toughness and ductility than impurity-minimized specimens.
Oxygen-doped specimens will show brittle fracture features and grain-boundary decohesion.
A low-impurity, single-phase baseline will exhibit high fracture resistance and ductility under the same loading conditions.
The proposed embrittlement behavior is most relevant near 700°C when temperature and loading rate permit segregation.
Analogous refractory HEA evidence supports an interstitial-to-segregation mechanism.
The magnitude of toughness loss and detailed microstructural evolution may vary with alloy composition and impurity concentration.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes reduced plasticity to reduced dislocation mobility from precipitation, while the mechanism also attributes segregation to depletion of strengthening interstitials and matrix weakening. These opposing effects on dislocation resistance are not reconciled.
